title: The whole Christ celebrates (CCC 1136–1144)
hook: heaven and earth, priest and people, all take part

segments.voice: Yesterday, liturgy: once a public work, now the people taking part in the work of God. Your line was the people's work. Where did you do your part out loud? Day one thousand eighty-eight.

A weekday morning Mass in a big church that's mostly empty. A priest at the altar. A woman in the front pew with a worn prayer book. A man near the back who came in on his way to work and kept his coat on. A teenager doing the readings, a little too fast. Rows and rows of empty wood. It looks like a small gathering. The Catechism sees something else happening. In its picture, that room is packed. Yesterday, the people's work. Today, who exactly the people are.
screen: `A MOSTLY EMPTY CHURCH.` → `A FEW PEOPLE, ROWS OF WOOD.` → `THE ROOM IS PACKED.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says the liturgy is the action of the whole Christ. It even gives the Latin, Christus totus: Christ the head, and his body, the Church, together. So who's there? First, heaven. The Catechism turns to the Apocalypse, where John is shown worship already going on in heaven: a throne, a Lamb "standing as it were slain," angels, elders, and every creature praising God. The living creatures there never stop saying, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come." The Catechism teaches that when the Church celebrates on earth, it joins that heavenly liturgy, already in progress. At Mass, as the great prayer over the bread and wine gets under way, the people sing holy, holy, holy, words close to what the angels sing in the prophet Isaiah. Second, the saints. The Catechism names Mary, the apostles, the martyrs and a great crowd of saints as taking part. Third, the whole community on earth. The Catechism says it's not the priest alone who celebrates. It's the whole body of Christ, united with its head. Every baptized person shares in it. Fourth, each in their own role. The ordained priest acts in a particular way, in the person of Christ. But readers, servers, singers: the Catechism counts all of them as having a real part. Each does their own job, and all of it is one act. So back to that weekday morning. A priest, a woman with a prayer book, a man in a coat, a nervous reader. In the Catholic understanding, also angels, saints, and the whole Church. Not a small gathering. A full house.
screen: `CHRISTUS TOTUS: HEAD AND BODY.` · `HEAVEN, ALREADY IN PROGRESS.` · `THE SAINTS AND THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `EACH IN THEIR OWN ROLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with the whole Church. Settle, and breathe. Wherever you are, let the room around you get bigger in your mind. Somewhere right now, people are gathered to pray, in big churches and small chapels, in hospitals, in kitchens. Hold them in mind for a moment. If you pray, you can join them with the angels' words from Isaiah: holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts. Say them slowly, knowing you aren't saying them alone. If you don't pray, simply sit with the thought that right now, other people, somewhere, are reaching toward something larger than themselves. The bell holds the time.
The whole Christ celebrates. Catholics believe the liturgy is the act of Christ and his whole body: heaven and earth, priest and people, angels and saints, all taking part. Today's word.
Your line: all of us. Today, when something feels small or lonely, ask who else might be in the room that you can't see. Day one thousand eighty-eight.

howItsDone: At Mass Catholics sing or say the Holy, holy, holy after the preface, near the start of the Eucharistic Prayer, which the Church understands as joining the praise of the angels and saints in heaven.

fork.setup: you're at a weekday Mass with a handful of people in a big empty church. who, in the Catechism's picture, is taking part?
options: the handful of people in the pews
Christ, the angels, the saints and the whole Church
fork.reveal: the Catechism calls the liturgy the act of the whole Christ, head and body, joined to the worship already going on in heaven.

original.note: Latin: the whole Christ, head and body together. The Catechism uses it for who celebrates the liturgy.

trapdoor: what you thought: the priest says Mass and the people attend.
what it means: Catholics believe Christ and his whole body celebrate together: heaven and earth, priest and people.
what a scholar hears: Christus totus, the whole Christ, joining the worship of the Apocalypse already going on in heaven.

sources.quoted: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.

notes: CCC paraphrased (1136 liturgy is the action of the whole Christ, Christus totus; 1137–1139 the heavenly liturgy of the Apocalypse, joined by the Church on earth; 1138 the Virgin Mary, apostles, martyrs and saints; 1140 the whole community, the Body of Christ united with its head; 1141 the common priesthood of the baptized; 1142 ordained ministers acting in the person of Christ; 1143 readers, servers, choir and other ministries; 1144 each according to their function). Confirm.

Isaiah 6:3 is paraphrased in the practice as 'holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts' (Challoner: 'Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory'). Kept without quotation marks; confirm the wording if it should be quoted.
'The person keeping the doors' as a liturgical role (usher) is the writer's addition to CCC 1143's list; a Keeper may cut it.
Confirm Challoner wording of Apocalypse 4:8 and 5:6 ('a Lamb standing as it were slain').
Original: 'Christus totus' appears in CCC 1136; Augustine is the source of the phrase (CCC 795), not named in the script.

Editor pass: the Sanctus was placed 'just before the prayers over the bread and wine', but the prayer over the offerings comes before it and the Sanctus belongs to the Eucharistic Prayer; teach and howItsDone corrected; dropped the unsourced 'that's why' causal link and 'the same words' (Isaiah 6:3 and the Mass text differ); cut the doorkeeper, which is not in CCC 1143's list; 'according to the Catechism, that room is packed' softened to the Catechism's picture.
